title: Providers, resources and the graph
summary: Provider requirements and version constraints, resources, data sources and references, and how Terraform orders its work from a dependency graph (and when it cannot see a dependency).

steps.title: Providers: the plugins that do the work
body: Terraform itself knows nothing about AWS or files. A **provider** is a plugin (a separate program) that knows one
API: `hashicorp/aws`, `hashicorp/azurerm`, `hashicorp/google`, `hashicorp/kubernetes`, `cloudflare/cloudflare`,
`datadog/datadog`, and the small utility ones this topic uses (`local`, `random`, `tls`, `time`, `null`, `archive`).
```hcl
terraform {
required_version = ">= 1.10"                 # which Terraform CLI may run this
required_providers {
aws = {
source  = "hashicorp/aws"                # registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws
version = "~> 6.0"                       # any 6.x, never 7.0
provider "aws" {
region = "eu-west-1"                         # configuration for the plugin; credentials come from the environment
`terraform init` finds a version that matches every constraint, installs it and records the exact version and its
checksums in `.terraform.lock.hcl`. From then on everyone (and CI) gets that same version until someone runs
`terraform init -upgrade` and commits the new lock file. **Never put credentials in a `provider` block**: use
environment variables, an SSO profile or the CI system's workload identity.

steps.prompt: Match each version constraint to the versions it allows.
pairs: anything from 2.0 up to, not including, 4.0
steps.explain: `~>` (the *pessimistic* operator) lets only the right-most given part grow. `~> 6.0` is the common choice for a provider: new features and fixes, no breaking major version. Pin exact versions in modules you publish only when you must; let the root configuration and its lock file decide.

steps.title: Resources, data sources and references
body: A **resource** block is something Terraform *manages*: it creates, updates and deletes it. Its **address** is
`TYPE.NAME` (`aws_s3_bucket.assets`, `local_file.motd`), unique in the module. Inside the block you set **arguments**;
afterwards the provider exposes **attributes**, some only known after creation (an `id`, an `arn`, an IP address).
A **data source** only *reads* something that exists already (managed elsewhere, or by another team):
```hcl
data "aws_vpc" "main" {
tags = { Name = "shop-prod" }
resource "aws_security_group" "db" {
name   = "shop-prod-db"
vpc_id = data.aws_vpc.main.id       # a reference: data.TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE
A **reference** such as `aws_security_group.db.id` or `data.aws_vpc.main.id` does two jobs: it passes the value, and
it tells Terraform the order. Terraform builds a **dependency graph** from all references and works through it,
creating independent resources in parallel (10 at a time by default, `-parallelism=N`) and destroying in reverse.

steps.prompt: Wire the alarm to the database: complete the references.
steps.explain: Resources are referenced as `TYPE.NAME.ATTRIBUTE`, data sources with the `data.` prefix. Both references also put the alarm *after* the database and the topic lookup in the graph.

steps.title: When Terraform cannot see a dependency
body: Terraform only knows about dependencies it can **see in references**. If two things are linked some other way (a file
path written as a string, an IAM policy that must exist before an app starts, a name typed twice), Terraform may run
them in parallel or in the wrong order. It often works on the laptop where the thing already existed, and fails on a
clean machine or in CI.
Two fixes, best first:
1. **Reference the value** instead of repeating it: `filename = local_file.settings.filename` rather than the same
string. The dependency is now visible and the two can never drift apart.
2. When there is no value to pass, say it outright with **`depends_on`**:
```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "app" {
# the app reads the policy at boot, but nothing here references it
depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.app_s3]
`depends_on` is a blunt tool: on a data source it delays the read until apply, so the plan shows less. Prefer a
reference whenever one exists. `terraform graph` prints the graph (in DOT; `dependent -> dependency`), and
`terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg` draws it where Graphviz is installed.

steps.title: It only works on Sam's laptop
prompt: `~/infra/site` is a fresh checkout. Sam says it applies fine for them. On your machine (and in CI) it does not.
1. `cd ~/infra/site` and run `terraform plan`. Read the error: which block fails, and why does the file not exist yet?
2. Fix the configuration so Terraform knows the data source must wait for `local_file.settings`. Do not create the
file by hand: a clean machine must work.
3. Plan and apply. Then look at the graph: `terraform graph | grep -- '->'`.
The check copies your `.tf` files to an empty folder and applies them there, like a CI runner would.

checks.name: a clean checkout applies
checks.cmd: rm -rf /tmp/fresh && mkdir /tmp/fresh && cp ~/infra/site/*.tf /tmp/fresh/ && cd /tmp/fresh && terraform init -input=false -no-color >/dev/null && terraform apply -auto-approve -input=false -no-color >/tmp/fresh.log 2>&1 && grep -q 'server_name shop.example.com;' build/nginx.conf || { tail -n 12 /tmp/fresh.log; exit 1; }
checks.fail: In an empty folder, `terraform apply` must work and write `build/nginx.conf` with `server_name shop.example.com;`. Make the data source depend on the resource that writes the file.

checks.name: your own folder is applied
checks.cmd: cd ~/infra/site && grep -q 'server_name shop.example.com;' build/nginx.conf && terraform plan -detailed-exitcode -input=false -no-color >/dev/null
checks.fail: Apply the fixed configuration in `~/infra/site` too, so `build/nginx.conf` exists and `terraform plan` shows no changes.

hints: The error is `Read local file data source error ... no such file or directory`: Terraform reads data sources during the plan, before `local_file.settings` has written anything.
The data source repeats the path as a string. Reference the resource instead, so the dependency is visible.
In the `data "local_file" "settings"` block: `filename = local_file.settings.filename`. Then `terraform plan` shows *will be read during apply*.
steps.explain: With the reference, the graph has `data.local_file.settings -> local_file.settings`, the plan says `data.local_file.settings will be read during apply (depends on a resource or a module with changes pending)`, and the order is right everywhere. Even simpler would be to drop the data source and use `local.settings` directly: reading back a file you just wrote is a sign the design can be flatter.

steps.prompt: An app server must not boot before an IAM policy that it uses at start-up exists. Nothing in the `aws_instance` block references the policy. What do you write?
options: Nothing: Terraform creates resources in the order they appear in the file
Put both resources in the same `.tf` file
steps.explain: The order of blocks and files does not matter at all: Terraform reads every `.tf` file in the folder as one configuration and orders work only by the graph. A hidden dependency needs `depends_on`. `-parallelism=1` only makes things slow; the order would still be undefined.

prompt: Given these references, in which order does `terraform apply` create the resources (one valid order)?
steps.explain: The VPC first (both others reference it), then the subnet and the security group (in parallel, in any order), then the instance, which references both. `terraform destroy` walks the same graph backwards: the instance goes first, the VPC last.
